newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss pledge wider hunt for Mobutu's bank fortunes.
newsitem.headline: Swiss pledge wider hunt for Mobutu's bank fortunes.

text.p: Switzerland, backtracking under international pressure, promised on Tuesday to widen a hunt for funds of Zaire's embattled ruler Mobutu Sese Seko after saying a previous check at Swiss banks had found no trace of any money.
The Federal Banking Commission, the country's banking watchdog, said it would expand its search in coming days, but suggested it was unlikely to find much wealth.

"I can't imagine that today, any Swiss bank would still have money from Mobutu. Such a bank would be extremely silly," Kurt Hauri, president of the independent commission, said in a veiled warning to bankers who may still have Mobutu's accounts.
"It should be in the interests of banks to be intelligent enough not to have money from a man like Mobutu. That would be extremely bad for the banks' reputation."
Hauri said his watchdog would nevertheless expand its hunt that has been limited so far to an informal check at big banks.
"The Banking Commission will expand the survey. We will order a more in-depth survey to include other banks in the next few days," he told Reuters.
Swiss media have estimated that Mobutu has some $4 billion stashed away in secret bank accounts in Switzerland. When asked, Swiss bankers regularly say they know nothing of Mobutu's funds.

But domestic critics suspect the worst of banks, whose accounts for such toppled strongmen as Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines and Haiti's Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier have been the subject of long legal battles.

"Swiss banks are a world champion in building up empires for crooks and then protecting them behind smokescreens," said Swiss sociologist Jean Ziegler, a Socialist member of parliament and a fierce critic of the government and banks.
Ziegler estimated that Mobutu had billions in secret numbered accounts in his name or in the names of family members.

"We're talking about companies owned by Mobutu's family, we're talking about very complicated structures and accounts of the whole clan," Ziegler said, predicting that the issue would explode into yet another Swiss banking scandal.

The German-language Swiss newspaper SonntagsZeitung said at the weekend that Mobutu's son Kongolo used Swiss banks to transact big deals for his trading firm's exports of tonnes of commodities like diamonds, gold and copper for its own account.
The paper said Kongolo Mobutu had close ties to Switzerland, where it said he attended school, had regularly sold diamonds in person and maintained friendly links to Geneva financiers.
It said he routinely told clients to transfer money to a Swiss account, possibly in Lausanne, where his father owns a sprawling luxury villa and underwent cancer surgery last year.
Hauri said his commission knew nothing of such dealings. But he said he could not rule out the possibility that Mobutu indeed had cash in Swiss banks "some months or some years ago."

The foreign ministry in Berne reiterated that it could look into freezing any Mobutu accounts only if a request came from Zaire authorities. But in a softening of stance, it suggested any new government in Zaire could get a quick hearing.
Rebels forceds who are pressing on to the capital Kinshasa have already asked Switzerland to freeze Mobutu's fortunes.

"If there were a new Zairean government, either democratically elected or whatever, and if this government sends us a demand, then it would be considered within our legal system," said foreign ministry spokeswoman Yasmine Chatila.

Speculation over Mobutu's assets comes in the middle of a simmering crisis over Swiss commercial dealings with Nazi Germany during World War Two and Jewish claims that its banks are sitting on the dormant assets of Jews killed by Hitler.

"Swiss banks always think the problem will go away after they say there is no such problem, like what they did with the Jewish money, with the Nazi gold. But world public opinion is catching up with them," Ziegler said.
